You will act as an expert summarizer. Fully summarize the following sets of texts, providing separate summaries for each text within each set.

--- START OF SET 1 ---

Text 1:
Sometimes it's nice to take a minute in the pew by yourself beforehand. You have this beautiful church probably almost all to yourself. Can you feel its energy resonating through you? Can you feel the majesty of the Lord's kingdom and how you're a part of it? Take a moment to kneel and pray with your head down and hands clasped together. Reflect on your faith and how you feel currently. Think about how you've been responding to God's call and how you've been living in the light of his love.

When the priest is ready for you, you'll probably see him there by his lonesome or someone else walk out just before you. Sit down either across from him or behind the screen — it's up to you whether you prefer to remain anonymous. He won't treat you any differently. Make the sign of the cross, saying: "Bless me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been 10 years since my last confession." This is traditional phrasing, but saying hello is fine too.

The Byzantine Rite can be a bit different: the priest may sit to your side and put his epitrachelion on your head, and say the Prayer of Absolution. The idea remains the same — follow the priest's lead. He may ask how long it's been since your last confession, how you are feeling, how your faith is going, and then what sins you would like to talk about with him and God. It is a casual conversation; there is zero pressure.

This part can be intimidating, but the priest has heard almost everything before. When he asks, mention your sins from the most serious to the least. Answer questions honestly, but you do not need to go into detail. If you don't remember the exact timeframe or motivation, that's fine. The goal is honesty and a heart in the right place. The priest may encourage you and offer ideas to bring you closer to God.

He will then ask you to make an Act of Contrition. One version says: "My God, I am sorry for my sins with all my heart... I firmly intend, with your help, to do penance, to sin no more, and to avoid whatever leads me to sin..." A Roman Catholic version says: "Oh my God, I am very sorry for having offended thee... I firmly resolve with the help of thy grace, to sin no more, and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen." After that, accept absolution and the penance given as an expression of repentance.

Text 2:
Hundreds of scientists around the world are looking for ways to treat heart attacks. But few started where Hedva Haykin has: in the brain. Haykin, a doctoral student at the Technion — Israel Institute of Technology in Haifa, wants to know whether stimulating a region of the brain involved in positive emotion and motivation can influence how the heart heals.
Late last year, in a small, windowless microscope room, she pulled out slides from a thin black box, one by one. On them were slices of hearts, no bigger than pumpkin seeds, from mice that had experienced heart attacks. Under a microscope, some of the samples were clearly marred by scars left in the aftermath of the infarction. Others showed mere speckles of damage visible among streaks of healthy, red-stained cells.
The difference in the hearts' appearance originated in the brain, Haykin explains. The healthier-looking samples came from mice that had received stimulation of a brain area involved in positive emotion and motivation. Those marked with scars were from unstimulated mice.
"In the beginning we were sure that it was too good to be true," Haykin says. It was only after repeating the experiment several times, she adds, that she was able to accept that the effect she was seeing was real. Haykin, alongside her supervisors at the Technion — Asya Rolls, a neuroimmunologist, and Lior Gepstein, a cardiologist — are trying to work out exactly how this happens. On the basis of their experiments so far, which have not yet been published, activation of this brain reward centre — called the ventral tegetal area (VTA) — seems to trigger immune changes that contribute to the reduction of scar tissue.
This study has its roots in decades of research pointing to the contribution of a person's psychological state to their heart health. In a well-known condition known as broken-heart syndrome, an extremely stressful event can generate the symptoms of a heart attack — and can, in rare cases, be fatal. Conversely, studies have suggested that a positive mindset can lead to better outcomes in those with cardiovascular disease. But the mechanisms behind these links remain elusive.
Rolls is used to being surprised by the results in her laboratory, where the main focus is on how the brain directs the immune response, and how this connection influences health and disease. Although Rolls can barely contain her excitement as she discusses her group's eclectic mix of ongoing studies, she is also cautious. Because of the often-unexpected nature of her team's discoveries, she never lets herself believe an experiment's results until they have been repeated multiple times.
For Rolls, the implications of this work are broad. She wants to provide an explanation for a phenomenon that many clinicians and researchers are aware of: mental states can have a profound impact on how ill we get — and how well we recover. Working out how this happens could enable physicians to tap into the power of the mind over the body. Understanding this could help to boost the placebo effect, enhance responses to vaccination, and even re-evaluate illnesses that have long been dismissed as psychologically driven.
She is part of a growing group of scientists mapping out the brain's control over the body's immune responses. There are multiple lines of communication between the nervous and the immune systems — from small local circuits in organs such as the skin, to longer-range routes beginning in the brain — with roles in a wide range of diseases, from autoimmunity to cancer.

Text 3:
The history of artificial intelligence (AI) began in antiquity, with myths, stories and rumors of artificial beings endowed with intelligence or consciousness by master craftsmen. The seeds of modern AI were planted by classical philosophers who attempted to describe the process of human thinking as the mechanical manipulation of symbols. This work culminated in the invention of the programmable digital computer in the 1940s, a machine based on the abstract essence of mathematical reasoning. This device and the ideas behind it inspired a handful of scientists to begin seriously discussing the possibility of building an electronic brain.
The field of AI research was founded at a workshop held on the campus of Dartmouth College during the summer of 1956. Those who attended would become the leaders of AI research for decades. Many of them predicted that a machine as intelligent as a human being would exist in no more than a generation, and they received millions of dollars to make this vision a reality.
Ultimately, the project was not successful. The researchers had underestimated the difficulty of the project. In 1973, in response to the criticism from James Lighthill and ongoing pressure from Congress, the U.S. and British governments cut off all undirected, exploratory research into AI. The first AI winter began.
In the early 1980s, AI research was revived by the commercial success of expert systems, a form of AI program that simulated the knowledge and analytical skills of human experts. By 1985, the market for AI had reached over a billion dollars. At the same time, Japan's fifth-generation computer project inspired the U.S. and British governments to restore funding for academic research. However, beginning with the collapse of the Lisp Machine market in 1987, AI once again fell into disrepute, and a second, longer-lasting AI winter began.
In the late 1990s and early 21st century, AI began to be used for logistics, data mining, medical diagnosis and other areas. The success was due to increasing computational power, greater emphasis on solving specific problems, new ties between AI and other fields, and a commitment by researchers to mathematical methods and scientific standards. Deep learning, a modern-day AI technique, became a buzzword in the 2010s and has since been applied to a wide range of tasks with remarkable success. The introduction of the transformer architecture in 2017 further accelerated progress, leading to the development of large language models (LLMs) with unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding and generation. This new era has sparked widespread public discussion about the societal impact of AI, including its potential benefits for science and creativity, as well as concerns regarding ethics, job displacement, and the need for responsible regulation.

Text 4:
Quantum computing represents a fundamentally new paradigm of computation. Unlike classical computers that store information in bits as either 0s or 1s, quantum computers use qubits. A qubit can exist as a 0, a 1, or a superposition of both states simultaneously. This property, along with another quantum phenomenon called entanglement, allows quantum computers to process a vast number of calculations at once. Entanglement is a counter-intuitive connection where two or more qubits become linked in such a way that their fates are intertwined, no matter the distance separating them. Measuring the state of one entangled qubit instantly influences the state of the other(s). These principles enable quantum computers to tackle certain problems that are intractable for even the most powerful classical supercomputers, such as factoring large numbers (Shor's algorithm) or simulating complex molecular interactions for drug discovery. However, building and operating quantum computers is incredibly challenging. Qubits are extremely fragile and sensitive to environmental noise, a phenomenon known as decoherence, which can destroy the quantum computation. Consequently, current quantum computers are small-scale and error-prone, often referred to as Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices.

--- END OF SET 1 ---
